title: Azure Virtual Machines Overview
description: Learn what Azure Virtual Machines are, how to choose VM sizes, and how availability sets keep your applications running.

data.text: An **Azure Virtual Machine** is a cloud-based computer you can control. Think of it like renting a physical server, but without having to plug in cables or manage the hardware. Azure takes care of the physical data center, and you get full control over the operating system, software, and settings.

VMs are useful when you need complete control over your environment. For example, you might use a VM to run a legacy application, host a custom database, or test software on a specific operating system version.

data.title: Common Reasons to Choose VMs
items: **Full control**: You choose the OS, patches, and installed software.
**Lift and shift**: Move existing on-premises servers to the cloud with little change.
**Custom workloads**: Run software that needs specific configuration or licensing.
**Development and testing**: Create clean, disposable environments quickly.

data.text: Azure offers many VM sizes, each optimized for different tasks. The size determines the number of CPUs, amount of RAM, and available disk space.

rows: Web servers, small databases, dev/test environments

data.text: Azure data centers have many servers, but sometimes hardware fails or maintenance is required. An **availability set** tells Azure to spread your VMs across different physical hardware, racks, and utility networks so that a single failure does not take down your entire application.

data.caption: How an availability set spreads VMs across fault domains.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Availability Set] --> B[Fault Domain 1]
    A --> C[Fault Domain 2]
    A --> D[Fault Domain 3]
    B --> E[VM 1]
    B --> F[VM 2]
    C --> G[VM 3]
    C --> H[VM 4]
    D --> I[VM 5]
    D --> J[VM 6]

terms.definition: A software-based computer running on Azure's physical hardware.
A predefined combination of CPU, memory, and disk capacity.
A configuration that spreads VMs across isolated hardware to improve uptime.

data.title: Create a Linux VM with Azure CLI
data.content: Run this command in Azure Cloud Shell or your local terminal with the Azure CLI installed.
data.code:
az vm create \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyLinuxVM \
  --image Ubuntu2204 \
  --size Standard_B1s \
  --admin-username azureuser \
  --generate-ssh-keys

data.title: Exercise: Choose a VM Size
data.description: Pick the right VM size for three different scenarios.
steps: A small blog that gets most traffic on weekends.
An in-memory cache storing 50 GB of frequently accessed data.
A nightly batch job that needs as much CPU as possible.
data.expectedOutcome: You can map workload patterns to B-series, E-series, and F-series VMs.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Azure VMs give you full control over a cloud-based computer.
Choose a VM size based on whether your workload needs more CPU, memory, or burst performance.
Availability sets spread VMs across isolated hardware to reduce downtime.
data.takeaway: Virtual Machines are the most flexible Azure compute option, but they also require the most management.
